The regex detectors can be used with any subcommand, while the sources defined in configuration are only for the `multi-scan` subcommand. The configuration format for sources can be found on Truffle Security's [source configuration documentation page](https://trufflesecurity.com/docs/connect-sources). Example GitHub source configuration and [options reference](https://docs.trufflesecurity.com/github#Fvm1I): ```yaml sources: - connection: '@type': type.googleapis.com/sources.GitHub repositories: - https://github.com/trufflesecurity/test_keys.git unauthenticated: {} name: example config scan type: SOURCE_TYPE_GITHUB verify: true ``` You may define multiple connections under the `sources` key (see above), and TruffleHog will scan all of the sources concurrently. To see debug logs for just one source, add `debug: true` to it. That source writes all of its debug logs, and every other source keeps the normal log level. This is useful when one source out of many is misbehaving: ```yaml sources: - connection: '@type': type.googleapis.com/sources.GitHub repositories: - https://github.com/trufflesecurity/test_keys.git unauthenticated: {} name: example config scan type: SOURCE_TYPE_GITHUB debug: true ``` To turn on debug logs for every source, use `--log-level=5` instead. ## S3 The S3 source supports assuming IAM roles for scanning in addition to IAM users. This makes it easier for users to scan multiple AWS accounts without needing to rely on hardcoded credentials for each account. The IAM identity that TruffleHog uses initially will need to have `AssumeRole` privileges as a principal in the [trust policy](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/how-to-use-trust-policies-with-iam-roles/) of each IAM role to assume. To scan a specific bucket using locally set credentials or instance metadata if on an EC2 instance: ```bash trufflehog s3 --bucket= ``` To scan a specific bucket using an assumed role: ```bash trufflehog s3 --bucket= --role-arn= ``` Multiple roles can be passed as separate arguments. The following command will attempt to scan every bucket each role has permissions to list in the S3 API: ```bash trufflehog s3 --role-arn= --role-arn= ``` ### Narrowing a scan to specific objects Large buckets often hold data that is never worth scanning, such as archives, media, and build artifacts. Two sets of flags keep those objects out of a scan. Both are matched against the object key before the object is downloaded, so a skipped object costs no GET request. Scan only the objects under one or more key prefixes: ```bash trufflehog s3 --bucket= --include-prefix=infra/ --include-prefix=services/ ``` Skip the objects under a key prefix: ```bash trufflehog s3 --bucket= --exclude-prefix=projects/archived/ ``` Both prefix flags can be used together to scan a subtree while leaving one part of it out. An object that matches an exclude prefix is always skipped, even if it also matches an include prefix: ```bash trufflehog s3 --bucket= --include-prefix=src/ --exclude-prefix=src/vendor/ ``` Prefixes are matched literally, not as globs, and they are not confined to a path boundary. `--include-prefix=log` matches both `logs/app.txt` and `logs-archive/app.txt`. File extensions are filtered separately. Write them without a leading dot: ```bash trufflehog s3 --bucket= --exclude-extension=zip --exclude-extension=mp4 ``` ```bash trufflehog s3 --bucket= --include-extension=tf --include-extension=yaml ``` Unlike the prefix flags, `--include-extension` and `--exclude-extension` cannot be combined, because naming the extensions to scan already excludes every other one. Using both fails at startup. Extension matching is case insensitive, so `--exclude-extension=zip` also skips `BACKUP.ZIP`. An object whose key has no extension at all, such as `Makefile`, matches no entry: it is skipped when `--include-extension` is set, and kept when only `--exclude-extension` is set. Two things to watch when using `--include-extension`. A dotfile counts as all extension, so `.env` has the extension `env` and any include list that leaves out `env` will skip every `.env` file in the bucket. Since `.env` files are a common place for secrets to sit, add `--include-extension=env` unless you mean to skip them. And only the last extension counts, so `backup.tar.gz` has the extension `gz`: `--exclude-extension=tar.gz` matches nothing, while `--exclude-extension=gz` works. These flags also apply to object keys only, not to files inside an archive. `--exclude-extension=mp4` skips `clip.mp4` sitting in the bucket, but not a `clip.mp4` packed inside `media.zip`. Excluding `zip` skips the archive entirely. TruffleHog asks S3 to list only the keys under the include prefixes, so a prefix that covers a small part of a large bucket is listed quickly. Exclude prefixes and extensions are applied after listing, so they cut the cost of downloading objects but not the cost of listing them. Prefixes and extensions are applied together. An object has to pass both to be scanned, so the command below scans `src/main.tf` but skips both `src/bundle.zip` and `docs/guide.tf`: ```bash trufflehog s3 --bucket= --include-prefix=src/ --exclude-extension=zip ``` These flags narrow the objects within a bucket. To narrow which buckets are scanned, use `--bucket` or `--ignore-bucket`, which unlike the prefix flags cannot be used together. Exit Codes: - 0: No errors and no results were found. - 1: An error was encountered. Sources may not have completed scans. - 183: No errors were encountered, but results were found. Will only be returned if `--fail` flag is used. ## :octocat: TruffleHog Github Action ### General Usage ``` on: push: branches: - main pull_request: jobs: test: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Checkout code uses: actions/checkout@v4 with: fetch-depth: 0 - name: Secret Scanning uses: trufflesecurity/trufflehog@main with: extra_args: --results=verified,unknown ``` In the example config above, we're scanning for live secrets in all PRs and Pushes to `main`. Only code changes in the referenced commits are scanned. If you'd like to scan an entire branch, please see the "Advanced Usage" section below. ### Shallow Cloning If you're incorporating TruffleHog into a standalone workflow and aren't running any other CI/CD tooling alongside TruffleHog, then we recommend using [Shallow Cloning](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-clone#Documentation/git-clone.txt---depthltdepthgt) to speed up your workflow. Here's an example of how to do it: ``` ... - shell: bash run: | if [ "${{ github.event_name }}" == "push" ]; then echo "depth=$(($(jq length <<< '${{ toJson(github.event.commits) }}') + 2))" >> $GITHUB_ENV echo "branch=${{ github.ref_name }}" >> $GITHUB_ENV fi if [ "${{ github.event_name }}" == "pull_request" ]; then echo "depth=$((${{ github.event.pull_request.commits }}+2))" >> $GITHUB_ENV echo "branch=${{ github.event.pull_request.head.ref }}" >> $GITHUB_ENV fi - uses: actions/checkout@v3 with: ref: ${{env.branch}} fetch-depth: ${{env.depth}} - uses: trufflesecurity/trufflehog@main with: extra_args: --results=verified,unknown ... ``` Depending on the event type (push or PR), we calculate the number of commits present. Then we add 2, so that we can reference a base commit before our code changes. We pass that integer value to the `fetch-depth` flag in the checkout action in addition to the relevant branch. Now our checkout process should be much shorter. ### Canary detection TruffleHog statically detects [https://canarytokens.org/](https://canarytokens.org/). ![image](https://github.com/trufflesecurity/trufflehog/assets/52866392/74ace530-08c5-4eaf-a169-84a73e328f6f) ### Advanced Usage ```yaml - name: TruffleHog uses: trufflesecurity/trufflehog@main with: # Repository path path: # Start scanning from here (usually main branch). base: # Scan commits until here (usually dev branch). head: # optional # Extra args to be passed to the trufflehog cli. extra_args: --log-level=2 --results=verified,unknown # Scan with a specific TruffleHog version (default: latest). version: # Docker image to pull. Override to use a registry mirror (default: ghcr.io/trufflesecurity/trufflehog). image: ``` If you'd like to specify specific `base` and `head` refs, you can use the `base` argument (`--since-commit` flag in TruffleHog CLI) and the `head` argument (`--branch` flag in the TruffleHog CLI). We only recommend using these arguments for very specific use cases, where the default behavior does not work. To upload results to GitHub code scanning instead, run TruffleHog directly with `--sarif` and pass the output to `github/codeql-action/upload-sarif`: ```yaml - name: TruffleHog run: trufflehog filesystem . --sarif --no-verification > results.sarif - name: Upload SARIF results uses: github/codeql-action/upload-sarif@v3 with: sarif_file: results.sarif ``` #### Advanced Usage: Scan entire branch ``` - name: scan-push uses: trufflesecurity/trufflehog@main with: base: "" head: ${{ github.ref_name }} extra_args: --results=verified,unknown ``` ## TruffleHog GitLab CI ### Example Usage ```yaml stages: - security security-secrets: stage: security allow_failure: false image: alpine:latest variables: SCAN_PATH: "." # Set the relative path in the repo to scan before_script: - apk add --no-cache git curl jq - curl -sSfL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/trufflesecurity/trufflehog/main/scripts/install.sh | sh -s -- -b /usr/local/bin script: - trufflehog filesystem "$SCAN_PATH" --results=verified,unknown --fail --json | jq rules: - if: '$CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"' ``` In the example pipeline above, we're scanning for live secrets in all repository directories and files. This job runs only when the pipeline source is a merge request event, meaning it's triggered when a new merge request is created. ## Pre-commit Hook TruffleHog can be used in a pre-commit hook to prevent credentials from leaking before they ever leave your computer. See the [pre-commit hook documentation](PreCommit.md) for more information. ## Custom Regex Detector (alpha) TruffleHog supports detection and verification of custom regular expressions. For detection, at least one **regular expression** and **keyword** is required. A **keyword** is a fixed literal string identifier that appears in or around the regex to be detected. To allow maximum flexibility for verification, a webhook is used containing the regular expression matches. TruffleHog will send a JSON POST request containing the regex matches to a configured webhook endpoint. If the endpoint responds with a `200 OK` response status code, the secret is considered verified. If verification fails due to network/API errors, the result is marked as unknown. Custom Detectors support a few different filtering mechanisms: entropy, regex targeting the entire match, regex targeting the captured secret, and excluded word lists checked against the secret (captured group if present, entire match if capture group is not present). Note that if your custom detector has multiple `regex` set (in this example `hogID`, and `hogToken`), then the filters get applied to each regex. [Here](examples/generic_with_filters.yml) is an example of a custom detector using these filters. The `verify` section is optional — if you omit it, matches are still reported as unverified, no webhook required. This makes Custom Detectors useful for flagging generic hardcoded secrets (e.g. `*.password=`, `*.secret=`) in config files like `.properties`, `.env`, or `.yaml` that TruffleHog's built-in, verified detectors won't otherwise catch. [Here](examples/generic_config_secrets.yml) is an example tuned for that use case. **NB:** This feature is alpha and subject to change. ### Regex Detector Example [Here](/pkg/custom_detectors/CUSTOM_DETECTORS.md) is how to setup a custom regex detector with verification server. ## Generic JWT Detection TruffleHog supports detection and verification of a subset of generic JWTs it finds. Specifically, if a JWT uses public-key cryptography rather than HMAC and the public key can be obtained, TruffleHog can determine whether the JWT is live or not. ## :mag: Analyze TruffleHog supports running a deeper analysis of a credential to view its permissions and the resources it has access to. ```bash trufflehog analyze ``` # :heart: Contributors This project exists thanks to all the people who contribute. [[Contribute](CONTRIBUTING.md)]. # :computer: Contributing Contributions are very welcome! Please see our [contribution guidelines first](CONTRIBUTING.md). We no longer accept contributions to TruffleHog v2, but that code is available in the `v2` branch. ## Adding new secret detectors We have published some [documentation and tooling to get started on adding new secret detectors](hack/docs/Adding_Detectors_external.md). Let's improve detection together! # Use as a library Currently, trufflehog is in heavy development and no guarantees can be made on the stability of the public APIs at this time. # License Change Since v3.0, TruffleHog is released under a AGPL 3 license, included in [`LICENSE`](LICENSE). TruffleHog v3.0 uses none of the previous codebase, but care was taken to preserve backwards compatibility on the command line interface. The work previous to this release is still available licensed under GPL 2.0 in the history of this repository and the previous package releases and tags. A completed CLA is required for us to accept contributions going forward.

repositories.name: ragflow
repositories.description: RAGFlow is an agent-native database: a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) engine that grew into context infrastructure.
repositories.readme:
Cloud | Documentation | Roadmap | Discord

📕 Table of Contents - 💡 [What is RAGFlow?](#-what-is-ragflow) - 🎮 [Get Started](#-get-started) - 🔥 [Latest Updates](#-latest-updates) - 🌟 [Key Features](#-key-features) - 🔎 [System Architecture](#-system-architecture) - 🏠 [Local Deployment](#-local-deployment) - 📚 [Documentation](#-documentation) - 📜 [Roadmap](#-roadmap) - 🏄 [Community](#-community) - 🙌 [Contributing](#-contributing)
## 💡 What is RAGFlow? [RAGFlow](https://ragflow.io/) is a leading open-source Retrieval-Augmented Generation ([RAG](https://ragflow.io/basics/what-is-rag)) engine that fuses cutting-edge RAG with Agent capabilities to create a superior context layer for LLMs. It offers a streamlined RAG workflow adaptable to enterprises of any scale. Powered by a converged [context engine](https://ragflow.io/basics/what-is-agent-context-engine) and pre-built agent templates, RAGFlow enables developers to transform complex data into high-fidelity, production-ready AI systems with exceptional efficiency and precision. ## 🎮 Get Started Try our cloud service at [https://cloud.ragflow.io](https://cloud.ragflow.io). For local deployment, see [Local Deployment](#-local-deployment).
## 🔥 Latest Updates - 2026-11-06 RAGFlow 1.0.0 released. - 2026-09-29 RAGFlow 1.0.0-rc1 released. - 2026-09-10 Added website content ingestion through sitemaps. - 2026-08-19 Introduced Knowledge Compilation to generate Wikis, Graphs, Trees, PageIndex, Mind Maps, Timelines, and Skills at the document and dataset levels. - 2026-08-19 Introduced Agentic RAG with Low, Medium, High, and Ultra thinking modes. - 2026-07-02 Added Google BigQuery data source ingestion and incremental synchronization. See the [full release notes](https://ragflow.io/docs/dev/release_notes) for more updates. ## 🌟 Key Features ### 🍭 **"Quality in, quality out"** - Deep document understanding-based knowledge extraction from unstructured data with complicated formats. - Finds "needle in a data haystack" of literally unlimited tokens. ### 🍱 **Template-based chunking** - Intelligent and explainable. - Plenty of template options to choose from. ### 🧩 **Knowledge Compilation** - Compile content at the document and dataset levels into structured knowledge artifacts. - Use compilation templates to generate Wikis, Graphs, Trees, PageIndex, Mind Maps, Timelines, and Skills for different knowledge organization and reuse needs. - Configure compilation models and processing rules, and view, update, and regenerate knowledge artifacts. ### 🧠 **Agentic Retrieval** - Perform multi-step retrieval for complex questions: the model analyzes the question and, when needed, breaks it down, retrieves knowledge, and verifies evidence. - Gather more complete context through multiple rounds of retrieval and reasoning to help generate well-grounded answers. - Choose Low, Medium, High, or Ultra thinking modes to control retrieval and reasoning depth according to question complexity. ### 🌱 **Grounded citations with reduced hallucinations** - Visualization of text chunking to allow human intervention. - Quick view of the key references and traceable citations to support grounded answers. ### 🍔 **Compatibility with heterogeneous data sources** - Supports Word documents, PowerPoint presentations, Excel spreadsheets, TXT files, images, PDFs, scanned copies, structured data, web pages, and more. ### 🛀 **Automated and effortless RAG workflow** - Streamlined RAG orchestration catered to both personal and large businesses. - Configurable LLMs as well as embedding models. - Multiple recall paired with fused re-ranking. - Intuitive APIs for seamless integration with business. ## 🔎 System Architecture
## 🏠 Local Deployment Local deployment supports both Docker deployment and launching from source. Docker is suitable for quick evaluation, integration testing, and production deployment, while launching from source is intended for RAGFlow development and debugging. Docker deployment does not require a Go compiler. Launching from source requires the Go version specified in `go.mod`; frontend development additionally requires Node.js and npm. ### 🐳 Docker Deployment #### 📝 Docker Deployment Prerequisites - Recommended starting configuration: 4 CPU cores, 16 GB RAM, and 50 GB of available disk space. Actual requirements depend on the document engine, data volume, parsing tasks, and concurrency. Local models and other optional components may require additional resources. - Docker ≥ 24.0.0, Docker Compose ≥ v2.26.1. > [!TIP] > If you have not installed Docker on your local machine (Windows, macOS, or Linux), see [Install Docker Engine](https://docs.docker.com/engine/install/). #### 🚀 Start up the server 1. If using Elasticsearch, set `vm.max_map_count` on the Docker host to at least 262144. This step is usually unnecessary with Infinity: > To check the value of `vm.max_map_count`: > > ```bash > sysctl vm.max_map_count > ``` > > If you use Elasticsearch and the value is below 262144, reset it: > > ```bash > # In this case, we set it to 262144: > sudo sysctl -w vm.max_map_count=262144 > ``` > > This change will be reset after a system reboot. To ensure your change remains permanent, add or update the `vm.max_map_count` value in **/etc/sysctl.conf** accordingly: > > ```bash > vm.max_map_count=262144 > ``` 2. Clone the repository: ```bash git clone https://github.com/infiniflow/ragflow.git ``` 3. Check out the release tag and start the server with Docker Compose: Enter the Docker deployment directory. ```bash cd ragflow/docker ``` Check out the `v1.0.0` release tag. ```bash git checkout v1.0.0 ``` Start the RAGFlow services and their dependencies. ```bash docker compose -f docker-compose.yml up -d ``` With the default MySQL configuration, the image entrypoint runs database migrations before starting Admin, Syncer, Ingestor, API, and other services. > In the RAGFlow open-source 1.0 release, DeepDoc uses CPU inference for layout analysis, OCR, and table recognition. 4. Check the server status after startup: Use `docker ps` to check the dependency services. After the dependencies show `healthy` and the RAGFlow container remains running, use the HTTP endpoint to determine whether RAGFlow is ready. The RAGFlow container itself does not define a Compose healthcheck. ```bash curl -f http://localhost/api/v1/system/healthz ``` After receiving an HTTP 200 response, open the Web UI. If you changed `SVR_WEB_HTTP_PORT`, replace the port in the health-check URL accordingly. If startup fails, inspect the container logs: ```bash docker logs --tail 50 ragflow-cpu ``` 5. In your web browser, enter the IP address of your server and log in to RAGFlow. > With the default settings, you only need to enter `http://IP_OF_YOUR_MACHINE` (**without** port number), because the default HTTP serving port `80` can be omitted when using the default configuration. 6. After signing in, add an LLM, embedding, and reranker on the model provider page, including the model name, service address, and API key. > For details, see [llm_api_key_setup](https://ragflow.io/docs/dev/llm_api_key_setup). _The show is on!_ See the [Quickstart guide](./docs/quickstart.mdx) for details. #### ⚙️ Docker Configuration and Adjustment Docker deployment uses `docker/.env` and `docker/docker-compose.yml`. Configure the image, ports, passwords, document engine, and model image source as described in the [Docker configuration guide](./docker/README.md). For platform support (note that macOS is not currently supported), see the [Go Docker image build and platform support guide](./docs/develop/build_docker_image.mdx). To build the Docker image from source, see the [Go Docker image build and platform support guide](./docs/develop/build_docker_image.mdx). For document-engine changes, configuration updates, restarting services, and retaining or removing existing data, follow the Docker configuration guide. ### 🔨 Launch from Source #### 📝 Source Build Prerequisites 1. Clone the repository and install the Go version specified in `go.mod` (currently Go 1.27), Clang 20, LLD 20, CMake ≥ 4.0, and PCRE2 development files. Go services depend on CGO and native static libraries; [build.sh](./build.sh) sets the required build parameters. ```bash git clone https://github.com/infiniflow/ragflow.git cd ragflow ``` 2. Run the dependency download script once to prepare everything the local Go server needs to build, run, parse documents and count tokens (`download_dev_deps.py` fetches the native static libraries and the runtime resources — cl100k vocabulary, DeepDoc `.ort` weights, embedding tokenizer assets): ```bash uv run tools/scripts/download_dev_deps.py ``` This is the local-dev one-stop: after one run the environment is ready, and already-present files are skipped so re-running never re-downloads. The image-facing counterpart `deps/download_deps.py` fetches the same runtime resources and skips the native `.a` files — run it only when building the dependency image or in CI, not for local development. `download_dev_deps.py` pulls and unpacks pdfium, pdf_oxide, office_oxide, and onnxruntime under `~/ragflow-native-libs`, and writes the cl100k vocabulary, DeepDoc models, and embedding tokenizer assets under `deps/`. It is a Python script; `uv run` installs its declared dependencies (`requests` and `huggingface-hub`) automatically. Skip this step if you have prepared the same resources by other means. When started from the repository root, Go services automatically find `internal/rag/res/deepdoc`; to start from another directory, set `DEEPDOC_MODEL_DIR` to its absolute path. 3. Build the services: ```bash ./build.sh --all ``` 4. Start the local dependency services and make sure the hosts and ports in **conf/service_conf.yaml** point to addresses accessible from the host. If using Elasticsearch, first set `vm.max_map_count` on the Docker host to at least `262144`. ```bash sudo sysctl -w vm.max_map_count=262144 docker compose --env-file docker/.env -f docker/docker-compose-base.yml up -d --wait es01 mysql minio nats kvrocks ``` 5. Migrate the database: ```bash ./bin/ragflow_server --migrate ``` 6. Start the four services in four separate terminals: Terminal 1: start Admin on port `9381`. ```bash ./bin/ragflow_server --admin ``` ```bash ./bin/ragflow_server --ingestor ``` Terminal 3: start Syncer. ```bash ./bin/ragflow_server --syncer ``` Terminal 4: start API on port `9380`. ```bash ./bin/ragflow_server --api ``` The startup modes work as follows: - `--migrate`: Runs database migrations and exits when complete. - `--admin`: Starts the Admin service for management and initialization operations. - `--ingestor`: Starts the Ingestor service for data ingestion and parsing tasks. - `--syncer`: Starts the Syncer service for external data source synchronization tasks. - `--api`: Starts the API service for the Web UI and SDKs. 7. Only when developing the frontend, install Node.js and npm, then start the React frontend: ```bash cd web npm install ``` After the services start, confirm that the API is ready: ```bash curl -f http://127.0.0.1:9380/api/v1/system/healthz ``` An HTTP 200 response indicates that the API is responding. See [Launch Service from Source](./docs/develop/launch_ragflow_from_source.md#5-verify-the-startup) for complete frontend and DeepDoc verification steps. See [Launch Service from Source](./docs/develop/launch_ragflow_from_source.md) for details. ## 📚 Documentation - [Quickstart](https://ragflow.io/docs/dev/) - [Configuration](https://ragflow.io/docs/dev/configurations) - [Release notes](https://ragflow.io/docs/dev/release_notes) - [User guides](https://ragflow.io/docs/category/user-guides) - [Developer guides](https://ragflow.io/docs/category/developer-guides) - [References](https://ragflow.io/docs/dev/category/references) - [FAQs](https://ragflow.io/docs/dev/faq) ## 📜 Roadmap See the [RAGFlow Roadmap 2026](https://github.com/infiniflow/ragflow/issues/12241). ## 🏄 Community - [Discord](https://discord.gg/NjYzJD3GM3) - [X](https://x.com/infiniflowai) - [GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/orgs/infiniflow/discussions) ## 🙌 Contributing RAGFlow flourishes via open-source collaboration. In this spirit, we embrace diverse contributions from the community. If you would like to be a part, review our [Contribution Guidelines](https://ragflow.io/docs/dev/contributing) first.

repositories.name: spotifast
repositories.description: Spotify, native and fast. One lightweight Rust app for your whole library, local playback, and Spotify Connect on Linux, macOS, and Windows.
repositories.readme:
Spotifast

Spotify, native and fast.
A lightweight music app for Linux, macOS, and Windows.

Download · Getting started · User guide · Contribute

Spotifast is a Spotify client written in Rust with [egui](https://www.egui.rs) and [fastframe](https://fastframe.dev), the framework behind a family of native desktop apps. It plays music through [Spotify Soloist](https://spotifast.rocks/soloist/) or the built-in [librespot](https://github.com/librespot-org/librespot) player, and has no browser engine. The interface includes complete [translations for all supported languages](docs/_reference/translating.md#languages-and-coverage). **Playback needs Spotify Premium.** Free accounts can browse and search, but cannot play music through Spotifast. ![Spotifast Home with the playlist library, recommendations, queue, and player visible](docs/screenshot.png)
Watch Spotifast in action https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/a5f669ce-b3b7-4f8e-9933-976a78876c7e
[Features](#your-music-on-your-desktop) · [Install](#install) · [First playback](#start-listening) · [Mini player](#the-winamp-mini-player) · [MilkDrop](#music-in-motion) · [Help](#guides-and-help) Since 0.15, setup leads with Spotify's [Soloist player](https://spotifast.rocks/soloist/), with guided key setup, one-time pairing and automatic renewal of expiring builds. New listeners and people updating see this choice once after sign-in on supported platforms. **Use the built-in player** keeps librespot, with Spotifast's EQ, visualizers, local files and full queue editing. The choice is remembered. On Linux with PipeWire, Soloist also supports Spotifast’s EQ and visualizers through a private audio route. [Native audio support](https://spotifast.rocks/soloist/#native-audio) adds EQ and visualizers on macOS 14.2 or newer, and visualizers on Windows 11, including MilkDrop. Windows Soloist playback does not support audible EQ. The Mac route keeps Soloist at full volume after redirecting its output, then applies Spotifast’s volume after the visualizers, including mute. Phone volume changes adjust that output level; Spotify’s indicator returns to 100%. Windows visuals keep their level as Soloist’s volume falls and stop only when it is muted. When enabled, Soloist appears as **This computer**; settings show the controls that apply to it. Turning it off restores the built-in player's preferences. While Soloist starts and its account is verified, the Spotify loading screen shows **Verifying Soloist…** and waits to accept playback commands. Setup takes three steps, and ends with choosing the named device in Spotify, with the built-in player available as a quiet alternative below the card. If Soloist stops later, a banner over the app says so while Spotifast restarts it, and offers **Try again** if that does not work. **Settings → Spotify Soloist → Spotify access** connects the separate Spotify session for Made for you, listening activity and Spotify lyrics without changing players. ## Your music, on your desktop | Feature | What you can do | |---|---| | **Library and search** | Browse playlists, Liked Songs, albums, artists, and podcasts. Discover upcoming albums on artist pages and open their countdown to pre-save. Search the catalogue and edit playlists you own. Copy a song's link, title, or artists from its menu. | | **Local files** | Play the local files your playlists list from a folder you choose in Settings, at any sample rate. Names show spaces and accents correctly, including in cached playlists. | | **Lyrics** | Spotify lyrics when the playback session is signed in, with LRCLIB as fallback. Temporary LRCLIB overloads retry and try search; older cached lyrics remain available during outages. | | **Spotify Connect** | Play on this computer or control playback on your other devices, including Google Cast speakers and groups. Cast devices appear as they are discovered; frequently and recently chosen outputs rise to the top. Remote volume keeps your chosen level while Spotify updates. | | **Queue** | Add songs to the queue, or choose **Play next** to put a song or selection first when playing on this computer. | | **Themes** | Choose light, dark, system appearance, or custom colours, with one theme for light mode and one for dark mode that switch with the system. On Omarchy, follow your desktop theme. | | **Desktop controls** | Use keyboard shortcuts and media keys. Keep music playing from the tray when supported by your desktop and settings, and start Spotifast with your computer, with its window or in the tray. | | **Winamp mini player** | Use classic skins with an equalizer, playlist, and animated sound displays. | | **MilkDrop** | Watch music-reactive visuals in a separate window or full screen. See platform availability below. | ## Install | Platform | Installation | |---|---| | **macOS** | `brew install --cask crmne/tap/spotifast`, or [download the Mac app](https://spotifast.rocks/download/#macos). | | **Arch Linux** | `yay -S spotifast-bin` | | **Windows** | The installer or a portable ZIP, for x64 and ARM, from the [Download page](https://spotifast.rocks/download/#windows). | | **Debian, Ubuntu** | The [DEB package](https://spotifast.rocks/download/#debian-and-ubuntu), then `sudo apt install ./spotifast_*.deb` | | **Fedora** | The [RPM package](https://spotifast.rocks/download/#fedora), then `sudo dnf install ./spotifast-*.rpm` | | **Other Linux** | Find Flatpak, AppImage, Nix, and other options on the [Download page](https://spotifast.rocks/download/#linux). | | **From source** | Follow [Build from source](https://spotifast.rocks/getting-started/#build-from-source) for dependencies and commands. | ## Start listening 1. Register Spotifast with Spotify, as the sign-in screen shows: in the [Spotify developer dashboard](https://developer.spotify.com/dashboard), click **Create app**, Spotify's name for this registration, with the redirect URI `http://127.0.0.1:8989/login` and **Web API** ticked. It takes about two minutes and gives you a Client ID. Spotify requires Premium on the account that registers, so a Free account can't do this step itself. [Getting started](https://spotifast.rocks/getting-started/#make-a-spotify-app) has the steps. 2. Paste the Client ID into Spotifast and choose **Sign in with Spotify**. Approve access in your browser, then return to the app to see your library. 3. To listen on this computer, open the device menu in the bottom player bar and choose **Set up playback here**, also available in Settings. 4. Complete the separate playback approval in your browser. Your computer appears as a Spotify Connect device named **Spotifast**. Library access and local playback have separate approvals. Spotifast remembers both using your computer's protected storage. See [Getting started](https://spotifast.rocks/getting-started/) for the full walkthrough and [How it connects](https://spotifast.rocks/how-it-connects/) for the details. ## The Winamp mini player A classic look for your music, with Winamp 2 `.wsz` and Windows Media Player `.wmz` skins, an equalizer, a playlist, and animated sound displays. Switch with **Ctrl+M** (**Cmd+Shift+M** on macOS), the shrink button, or Settings. The spectrum analyser and oscilloscope also work in the collapsed title bar.

[Explore the mini player](https://spotifast.rocks/winamp/), including skins, window sizes, controls, and the return to the main player. ## Music in motion MilkDrop reacts to music playing on this computer, with more than 10,000 presets downloaded on first use. Open it from the visualiser button, Settings, or the mini player's **V** menu. ![MilkDrop visualiser displaying coloured concentric patterns in Spotifast](docs/assets/images/milkdrop-poster.jpg) Included on **Linux**, **macOS**, and **Windows Intel/AMD** builds. It is not included in the Windows on ARM download. [Read the MilkDrop guide](https://spotifast.rocks/milkdrop/) for presets, controls, and fullscreen mode. ## Guides and help The complete guide lives at **[spotifast.rocks](https://spotifast.rocks/)**. | You want to… | Read | |---|---| | Sign in, set up playback, or configure themes, fonts, and proxies | [Getting started](https://spotifast.rocks/getting-started/) | | Learn shortcuts, command-line controls, and updates | [Everyday use](https://spotifast.rocks/using-spotifast/) | | Check storage sizes, clear cached audio and find stored files | [Settings and files](https://spotifast.rocks/settings-and-files/) | | Understand scrolling performance and reduce loading delays | [Make it even faster](https://spotifast.rocks/make-it-even-faster/) | | Fix "Spotify refused the audio key" or "Spotify is being slow" | [When something goes wrong](https://spotifast.rocks/troubleshooting/) | | Understand what is stored and sent | [Privacy](https://spotifast.rocks/privacy/) · [How it connects](https://spotifast.rocks/how-it-connects/) | | Check Spotify and librespot limitations | [What Spotify allows](https://spotifast.rocks/what-spotify-allows/) | | Is it safe for my account? | [Account safety](https://spotifast.rocks/what-is-spotifast/#account-safety) | | Report a bug or propose a feature | Read [Contributing](CONTRIBUTING.md), then use the [issue forms](https://github.com/crmne/spotifast/issues/new/choose). | ## Contributing Read [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) before opening an issue or pull request. To look at the interface without a Spotify account, run: ```sh cargo run --features demo -- --demo ``` Translations live in `assets/i18n/`; see [Translating Spotifast](docs/_reference/translating.md). Release packaging is described in [PACKAGING.md](PACKAGING.md). ## More native apps **Want WhatsApp just as fast and native?** [ZapFast](https://zapfast.rocks) is Spotifast's sibling. Both are built on [fastframe](https://fastframe.dev). ## Spotify Connect updates With local playback enabled, Spotify pushes changes from other devices over Spotifast's existing Connect session. Playback changes trigger a refresh. Volume-only changes appear directly for the active playback device without an extra request; an unconfirmed volume change made in Spotifast takes precedence. Push-triggered refreshes are at least a second apart and wait for a pending playback read to finish. Changes received during that read are folded into one follow-up. Connect pushes are ignored when this computer is the active device both before and after; position-only updates cause no requests. Regular polling remains the fallback. ## Sonos playback Sonos speakers use the Spotify Connect session for playback control. Enable local playback first, then select the speaker in the device picker. ## Acknowledgements Spotifast uses [librespot](https://github.com/librespot-org/librespot), [egui](https://www.egui.rs), [fastframe](https://fastframe.dev), the [Inter](https://rsms.me/inter/) typeface (OFL), and [Lucide](https://lucide.dev) icons (ISC). Spotifast is an independent project and is not affiliated with Spotify. Spotify is a trademark of Spotify AB. Licensed under the [MIT License](LICENSE). ## Star history

repositories.name: substrate
repositories.description: Agent Substrate: the core system
repositories.readme:
# Agent Substrate **Zero-trust sandboxing for millions of agents on Kubernetes.** [![License](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-Apache_2.0-blue.svg)](https://opensource.org/licenses/Apache-2.0) [![Release](https://img.shields.io/github/v/release/agent-substrate/substrate)](https://github.com/agent-substrate/substrate/releases) [![CI](https://github.com/agent-substrate/substrate/actions/workflows/pr-workflow.yaml/badge.svg?branch=main)](https://github.com/agent-substrate/substrate/actions/workflows/pr-workflow.yaml?query=branch%3Amain) [![govulncheck](https://github.com/agent-substrate/substrate/actions/workflows/govulncheck.yaml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/agent-substrate/substrate/actions/workflows/govulncheck.yaml) [![GitHub stars](https://img.shields.io/github/stars/agent-substrate/substrate?style=flat)](https://github.com/agent-substrate/substrate/stargazers) [Quickstart](#quickstart-development) · [Security](docs/security/security.md) · [Architecture](docs/concepts/architecture.md) · [Contributing](CONTRIBUTING.md)
## What is Agent Substrate? Agent Substrate is a security-hardened, zero-trust runtime for sandboxed agents, engineered to safely run millions of agents and tools with 10x higher density than standard containers. Purpose-built for the era of autonomous agents, Substrate delivers fast resume operations in less than 500ms, with more than 500 activations per second. Agents get isolated compute, identity, networking, and storage. Sensitive credentials are kept out of reach from untrusted code. It supports multiple sandbox technologies, including microVMs and gVisor, while enabling a consistent lifecycle and management of all sandboxes. At its core, Agent Substrate maps a larger set of “actors” (stateful workloads such as agents) onto a smaller pool of ready “workers”. Because agents spend most of their lives waiting on models, tools, or humans, Substrate snapshots idle actors out of memory and restores them when a request arrives. Substrate is a low-opinion runtime, not an agent SDK. The workloads it runs do not have to be AI agents, though autonomous, untrusted, mostly-idle agents are the target for its isolation and scheduling model. It runs on standard Kubernetes: Pods, autoscaling, NetworkPolicies. It adds agent-specific scheduling, snapshotting, identity, and network mediation. This allows agentic, inference, training, and reinforcement learning workloads to share one infrastructure plane. ## Security Model Substrate treats every actor as untrusted and mutually hostile, so tenants can share physical nodes without sharing a security boundary. Every control operates within the cold-start and resume budget. See the [Security Guide](docs/security/security.md) for the full list of security principles and threat model. * **Always sandboxed, VM-grade boundaries:** Every actor runs inside a dedicated [gVisor](https://gvisor.dev/) (`runsc`) or [Cloud Hypervisor](https://www.cloudhypervisor.org/) microVM sandbox with segregated compute, network, and storage. Plain Linux containers are not supported. * **Per-agent cryptographic identity:** Every active actor receives a short-lived [SPIFFE](https://spiffe.io/) X.509 certificate by default, and the egress gateway can mint per-actor JWTs on demand when an egress policy calls for one. Both carry the actor identity and atespace (the Substrate namespace grouping), and are designed to federate with external identity systems. * **Zero credentials in the sandbox:** Actors never hold actor identity JWTs/certs, API keys, or cloud tokens. The built-in egress gateway ([`atenet-egress`](docs/guides/egress-credential-injection.md)) injects credentials into approved outbound requests outside the sandbox, so a prompt-injected or compromised agent has nothing to exfiltrate. * **Default-deny networking:** Actors start with a private network stack, no inbound path except through the ingress router (`atenet-router`), no lateral actor-to-actor or control-plane access, and outbound traffic [restricted by the egress gateway](docs/guides/egress-traffic.md). * **Pluggable policy at the edge:** The egress gateway acts as an external Policy Enforcement Point (PEP) that is fully replaceable, allowing you to attach your own authorization, DLP, prompt-injection scanning, or cloud IAM policy engine without placing policy code inside the untrusted sandbox. ## Performance & Multiplexing [![Agent Substrate Demo](https://img.youtube.com/vi/ZEzkCFJkzjY/hq1.jpg)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZEzkCFJkzjY) *Watch the Agent Substrate cluster multiplex ~250 stateful actors across just 8 physical pods.* This demo highlights the core developer experience and "Agentic Infrastructure" capabilities of Substrate: 1. **Actor Teleport:** Suspend and resume actors onto any available worker in the pool, when needed. 2. **Full-State Persistence:** Working memory (RAM) and filesystem state are captured in snapshots and restored intact across hibernation cycles, without losing in-flight sessions or tool state. 3. **10x–30x Oversubscription:** Multiplex a large registry of stateful actors onto a small pool of warm worker pods, paying for compute only while an agent is actively thinking or executing a tool. To reproduce this demo in your own cluster, see the **[Counter Demo](demos/counter/README.md)**. For more walkthroughs, visit the **[agent-substrate YouTube channel](https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCN9PPqlTtVxlcpbQ-NWpfZQ)**. ## Star History ## Framework Agnostic & Compatibility Agent Substrate is **framework and agent harness agnostic**. Because it runs standard OCI container images inside gVisor or microVM sandboxes and enforces security outside the workload, it hosts agents built on any stack without SDK changes: * **Agent Development Kit (ADK):** Preserves session state across invocations as actor state. * **LangChain:** Drop-in execution environment for LangChain agents and tool calls. * **Claude Code, Codex, and Antigravity:** High-density, stateful coding environments that keep system and filesystem state across sessions while isolating untrusted code execution. * **Model Context Protocol (MCP):** Deploy sandboxed MCP servers as Substrate Actors with per-actor identity and egress controls. ## Ecosystem & Examples * **[Agent Executor](https://github.com/google/ax):** A distributed agent runtime that demonstrates building a secure, hyper-scalable agent harness on Agent Substrate (see the [announcement blog](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/ai-machine-learning/agent-executor-googles-distributed-agent-runtime) and [integration guide](https://github.com/google/ax#2-deploy-the-control-plane)). * **[kagent](https://github.com/kagent-dev/kagent):** A CNCF Sandbox project and Kubernetes-native framework for building, deploying, and managing AI agents that uses Agent Substrate to run sandboxed, stateful agent workloads (see the [announcement blog](https://kagent.dev/blog/the-future-of-kagent)). ## Status and compatibility Agent Substrate has reached 1.0. We are committed to compatibility and stability of the public API, CLI, and configuration formats. We will continue to add new features, but we will not break existing APIs or configuration formats without a major version bump. See "Compatibility and schema evolution" in [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) for more details. ### Supported Kubernetes Releases Currently we aim to support the [latest stable release](https://kubernetes.io/releases/) of Kubernetes, and the previous minor release. ## Community For announcements, technical discussions, and community support, please join the **[ate-dev](https://groups.google.com/g/ate-dev)** Google Group. We host a weekly community meeting every Thursday from 10:00am - 11:00am PST. - Video call link: https://meet.google.com/uhq-cxvn-dhy - Or dial: (US) +1 253-289-6971 PIN: 787 664 574 59# - More phone numbers: https://tel.meet/uhq-cxvn-dhy?pin=9044088223662 - [Meeting notes](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1obSIvfcafLNniLYTQCcT2eCgxHqa2AQ3Ga7YTsju49s) for the weekly sync meeting - [Recordings and transcripts](https://drive.google.com/corp/drive/u/0/folders/1rX1S6vPxPrR8dA1lEBuBEXkGKjHtG-mL) of all community meetings We also have channels in the CNCF slack; [request an invite here](https://slack.cncf.io/) if you don't have access. - [#substrate-users](https://cloud-native.slack.com/archives/C0B6RCAJULW) to discuss using substrate. - [#substrate-dev](https://cloud-native.slack.com/archives/C0B6M3E2J3D) to discuss developing substrate. ## Developing Please see [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) for guidelines on contributing to the project. We welcome contributions of all kinds, but the project is VERY young. Our immediate focus is on building out the core system and demos, so we may not be able to review or merge contributions that don't align with those goals in the near term. ## Quickstart (Development) To quickly set up the complete environment: 1. Make sure you have [Go](https://go.dev/doc/install), [`kubectl`](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/tools/), and [`docker`](https://www.docker.com/) installed and configured on your dev machine. We will automatically manage other dependencies via Go, including [`kind`](https://kind.sigs.k8s.io/). A Linux host that will run more than about a thousand sandboxes also needs a larger kernel neighbor table (`net.ipv4.neigh.default.gc_thresh1/2/3` = 4096/16384/32768); `hack/create-kind-cluster.sh` warns when the host is at the default of 1024. 2. Run the following steps: ```shell # create cluster and local registry hack/create-kind-cluster.sh # make ate-setup target the kind cluster; set this in every shell that runs # ate-setup, including for the demo walkthroughs export ATE_INSTALL_KIND=true # install Substrate go run ./cmd/ate-setup deploy ate-system --credential-provider='{"name":"k8s.io"}' \ --ingress-allowed-spiffe-ids=spiffe://cluster.local/ns/ate-system/sa/atenet-client # install counter demo go run ./cmd/ate-setup deploy demo counter # install kubectl-ate go install ./cmd/kubectl-ate # create a counter actor in the demo's atespace (--template names the # actor template, resolved in the actor's atespace) kubectl ate create actor my-counter-1 -a ate-demo-counter --template counter # serve a local proxy on port 8000 that sends requests to the actor through the # network router kubectl ate proxy actor my-counter-1 -a ate-demo-counter ``` > [!IMPORTANT] > `{"name":"k8s.io"}` deploys the bundled credential provider with an empty, > default-deny namespace policy. Before an actor can have a credential > injected, grant its atespace the namespaces whose Secrets it may read; see > [Enable it](docs/guides/egress-credential-injection.md#enable-it). 3. In a **separate terminal**, send an HTTP request to increment the counter: ```shell curl -X POST -i http://localhost:8000/ ``` ### Custom Setup and Deployment You can deploy or cleanup specific Agent Substrate components using the installation script. See `go run ./cmd/ate-setup` for all options. ```bash # Re-deploy only ate-apiserver of the ATE system go run ./cmd/ate-setup deploy apiserver # Delete everything (core system and all demos) go run ./cmd/ate-setup delete all ``` ### Tearing down local `kind` resources If you need to delete the local `kind` cluster and its registry (if it was created by `hack/create-kind-cluster.sh`): ```bash ./hack/delete-kind-cluster.sh ``` ### GKE Quickstart To deploy on Google Kubernetes Engine, follow the official [GKE Installation Guide](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/ai-ml/install-overview-substrate). It lists the prerequisites and gives the one-line installer command. The installer's source and detailed options are in [substrate-gke](https://github.com/ai-on-gke/substrate-gke). ## Demos We provide several sample applications demonstrating Agent Substrate's capabilities: 1. **[Counter Demo](demos/counter/README.md)**: A stateful Go HTTP server demonstrating state preservation across suspends/resumes, and on-demand actor resumption and routing via the Substrate router. 2. **[Sandbox Demo (Antigravity)](demos/sandbox/README.md)**: A secure, sandboxed execution environment (running Alpine Linux) that allows arbitrary shell execution while preserving filesystem state across sessions. 3. **[Claude Code Multiplex](demos/claude-code-multiplex/README.md)**: Demonstrates oversubscribing physical hardware by multiplexing multiple Claude Code agents onto a limited pool of workers. 4. **[Multi-Template](demos/multi-template/README.md)**: Two `ActorTemplate`s running different binaries share one `WorkerPool`, even though the templates live in different atespaces. 5. **[Request Parking](demos/parking/README.md)**: An oversubscribed pool where the router holds inbound requests until a worker frees up, instead of returning `503`. ### Documentation & Guides * [Architecture](docs/concepts/architecture.md): How the control plane, node supervisor, and networking stack fit together. * [API Configuration Guide](docs/reference/api-guide.md): Detailed reference for configuring WorkerPools, ActorTemplates, Secrets, and Volumes. * [Full CLI Documentation](docs/reference/kubectl-ate.md): Installation and usage for `kubectl-ate`. * [Glossary](docs/reference/glossary.md): Core terms (Actor, Atespace, ActorTemplate, WorkerPool, Worker, ate-api-server, atenet, atelet, ateworker) and how they relate. * [Integration Repositories](docs/project/integration-repos.md): Where integrations live, how their repositories are named, and how fixes flow back to core. * [Observability Guide](docs/guides/observability.md): Guide to actor logging, metrics, and distributed tracing. * [Extending Substrate](docs/security/extensibility.md): How to augment or replace the built-in ingress and egress gateways. * [Authentication Guide](docs/guides/authentication.md): Which credential people, pods and CI jobs should use with the Substrate API, and how to trust more JWT issuers. * [Actor JWTs](docs/guides/actor-jwts.md): What an actor JWT contains, how relying parties verify it, and how to rotate the signing key. * [Federating actor JWTs](docs/guides/actor-jwt-federation.md): Serve the actor JWT issuer publicly and set up a relying party outside the cluster to trust it. * [Rotating the actor JWT signing key](docs/guides/actor-jwt-key-rotation.md): The rotation steps, how long to wait between them, and replacing a compromised key. * [Egress Traffic](docs/guides/egress-traffic.md): Which protocols an Actor may reach the outside world with and which are blocked. * [Enabling man-in-the-middle (MITM) interception for Actor Egress policy](docs/guides/egress-trust-bundle.md): Egress policies such as header injection depend on MITM interception of Actor traffic. This guide explains how an Actor should be configured to enable interception. * [Request Parking](docs/concepts/request-parking.md): How the router parks requests through transient worker-pool saturation. * [Sandbox Asset Cache](docs/concepts/sandbox-asset-cache.md): How a node caches the sandbox binaries actors run on, decides which runtimes it needs, and evicts to a budget. * [Upgrade Runbook](docs/guides/upgrade.md): Upgrade a running install to a newer supported release, and roll back if needed. * [Node Storage](docs/guides/node-storage.md): How to give snapshot I/O its own disk. * [Security Guide](docs/security/security.md): Security overview, security principles, and threat modeling. * [Benchmarking Guide](docs/guides/benchmarking.md): Locust-based load tests, monitoring stack, and the orchestrated benchmark harness. ## Tour ### Commands * `cmd/ateapi`: The core control plane API server exposing gRPC endpoints to manage actor and worker lifecycles. * `cmd/atelet`: A node-level DaemonSet that supervises physical worker pods, coordinates snapshotting, and manages state transfers. * `cmd/atecontroller`: A Kubernetes controller that reconciles WorkerPool custom resources. * `cmd/ate-idp-server`: Serves the OpenID discovery document and key set that relying parties use to verify actor JWTs. * `cmd/atenet`: A combined networking controller providing Envoy routing and proxy sidecars. * `cmd/ateworker-gvisor`: An interior-pod helper running inside sandboxed worker pods to execute `runsc` checkpoint and restore commands. * `cmd/ateworker-microvm`: The microVM peer of `ateworker-gvisor`, running actors as cloud-hypervisor VMs. * `cmd/podcertcontroller`: A "polyfill" that provides Pod Certificate signers that will eventually ship in upstream Kubernetes (with different names). * `cmd/kubectl-ate`: A CLI tool for managing Agent Substrate resources. See its [README](docs/reference/kubectl-ate.md). * `cmd/benchmarking`: Synthetic workloads used by the load tests, including `glutton`, which consumes RAM, disk, and file descriptors on demand. * `demos/`: Sample applications demonstrating Agent Substrate capabilities.

repositories.readme:
# v2.15 is out! 🥳 [Download Now ⬇️](https://github.com/upscayl/upscayl/releases/latest)

Special thanks to our sponsors:

Warp, the intelligent terminal for developers
Use images as AI context in your terminal!
Requestly - Free & Open-Source alternative to Postman
All-in-one platform to Test, Mock and Intercept APIs.
# ![Frame 111](https://github.com/upscayl/upscayl/assets/25067102/d1b4af3c-aade-4bc9-97d0-cf88db679931)

# 🆙 Upscayl #### Free and Open Source AI Image Upscaler Upscayl lets you enlarge and enhance low-resolution images using advanced AI algorithms. Enlarge images without losing quality. It's almost like magic! 🎩🪄 **https://upscayl.org**
# Contents - [👨‍💻 Installation](#-installation) - [🐧 Linux](#-linux) - [🍎 macOS](#-macos) - [🐌 Windows](#-windows) - [👨‍🏫 Documentation - Tutorials and Guides](#-documentation---tutorials-and-guides) - [⚖️ Demo Results (Before and After)](#%EF%B8%8F-results) - [🤫 Roadmap](#-roadmap) - [🛠 Developing Upscayl](#-development) - [🤓 FAQ](#-faq) - [🎁 Donate and support the project](#-donate) - [❤ Credits](#-credits) # 👨‍💻 Installation > [!IMPORTANT] > You'll need a Vulkan compatible GPU (Graphics Card) to upscale images. Many iGPUs (integrated graphics) do not work but, no harm in trying :) ## 🐧 Linux Upscayl should be available on the software listings of most Linux operating systems. Your distro's Store app might also support the [Flatpak](https://flatpak.org/setup) or Snap version. ### 💼 Portable Method 1. Go to [releases section](https://github.com/upscayl/upscayl/releases/latest) or [our official website](https://upscayl.org/). 2. Download the `upscayl-x.x.x-linux.AppImage` file. 3. Right Click AppImage -> Go to Permissions tab -> Check 'allow file to execute' and then double click the file to run Upscayl. *You can also choose to install using other formats like RPM (Fedora), DEB (Debian/Ubuntu based), and ZIP (Any x86 Linux OS).* ## 🍎 macOS (MacOS 12 and later) Link 1. Go to [releases section](https://github.com/upscayl/upscayl/releases/latest) or [our official website](https://upscayl.org/). 2. Download the `upscayl-x.x.x-mac.dmg` file. 3. Double click dmg, drag Upscayl icon into Applications folder. 4. Open Finder, click 'Applications' tab in the left sidebar. Find Upscayl and right click on it. Select 'Open'. 5. In the window that appears, press 'Open' yet again. ### 🍺 Homebrew `brew install --cask upscayl` ## 🐌 Windows (Windows 10 and later) 1. Go to [releases section](https://github.com/upscayl/upscayl/releases/latest) or [our official website](https://upscayl.org/). 2. Download the `upscayl-x.x.x-win.exe` file. 3. Double click exe file to launch. 4. If you get a SmartScreen warning - click 'More Info' and then 'Run Anyway' OR press 'YES' on the unverified publisher dialog. 5. Follow the installation steps. 6. Profit! # 👨‍🏫 Documentation - Tutorials and Guides Check out our Documentation [here](https://docs.upscayl.org/). - [Try out even more new models!](https://github.com/upscayl/custom-models) - [Convert your own models](https://github.com/upscayl/upscayl/wiki/%F0%9F%96%A5%EF%B8%8F-Model-Conversion---Create-more-AI-models!) - [Compatibility List](https://github.com/upscayl/upscayl/wiki/Compatibility-List) - [Troubleshooting](https://github.com/upscayl/upscayl/wiki/Troubleshooting) # ⚖️ Results Check out Upscayl before/after comparisons [here](COMPARISONS.MD). # 🤫 Roadmap You can track all the progress here: https://github.com/orgs/upscayl/projects/1 - Fix bugs - Make the whole world use FOSS (WIP 🚧) # 🛠 Development I recommend using Volta: https://volta.sh for installing Node.js. Download and install volta, then do: `volta install node`. ## 🏃 Running > [!NOTE] > If you are not willing to install [git](https://git-scm.com/downloads), you can skip the first line, download [the source zip](https://github.com/upscayl/upscayl/archive/refs/heads/main.zip) and extract it to `upscayl` instead and carry on with the rest of the instructions. ```sh git clone https://github.com/upscayl/upscayl cd upscayl # INSTALL DEPENDENCIES npm install # RUN THE DEVELOPMENT SERVER LOCALLY ## YOUR LOGS WILL NOW APPEAR IN THE TERMINAL npm run start ``` ## 🏗️ Building ```sh # INSTALL DEPENDENCIES npm install # PACKAGE THE APP npm run dist # PUBLISH THE APP, MAKE SURE TO ADD GH_TOKEN= IN SHELL # ONLY DO THIS IF YOU'RE A MAINTAINER npm run publish-app ``` # 🤓 FAQ - **How does Upscayl work?** - Upscayl uses AI models to enhance your images by guessing what the details could be. It uses Real-ESRGAN and Vulkan architecture to achieve this. [Our backend](https://github.com/upscayl/upscayl-ncnn) is fully open-source under the AGPLv3 license. - **I don't see a drastic change in my upscaled image. Why is that?** - Upscayl can enhance low resolution images and images that are pixelated but it cannot de-blur or do focus adjustment on your image. If your image is out-of-focus or totally blurred, Upscayl is not the right tool for it. Please use images that are similar to the [examples we've given here.](COMPARISONS.MD) - **Is there a CLI available?** - The CLI tool is called [upscayl-ncnn](https://github.com/upscayl/upscayl-ncnn). - **Do I need a GPU for this to work?** - Yes, unfortunately. NCNN Vulkan requires a Vulkan-compatible GPU. Upscayl won't work with **most** iGPUs or CPUs. But hey, no harm in trying ;) - @Wyrdgirn has contributed a workaround for Windows and Linux in [#390](https://github.com/upscayl/upscayl/issues/390)! Nobody knows how to manipulate the macOS and Haiku frameworks... - **I stopped the magic Batch Upscayl and my images haven't been processed, compressed, or are in the wrong scale!** - When a model doesn't support an action, Upscayl will finish upscayling all the images first before post-processing them. What this means is that you should simply **wait** for the process to finish. - **How can I contribute?** - You can report issues, fix code and add features by submitting PRs, or donate! 😊 - **What's the GPU ID for?** - It is for selecting which GPU to use. The specific procedure is detailed in the [Wiki](https://github.com/upscayl/upscayl/wiki/Guide). - Note that for Windows systems, if Upscayl is not set to performance mode, the system may override this setting. - **Where do I find more models?** - More models can be taken from here: https://github.com/upscayl/custom-models # 🎁 Donate # ❤ Credits - Real-ESRGAN for their wonderful research work. [Real-ESRGAN: Copyright (c) 2021, Xintao Wang](https://github.com/xinntao/Real-ESRGAN/) - @JanDeDinoMan, @xanderfrangos, @Fdawgs, @keturn for their code contributions - @aaronliu0130 for providing community support :) - Helaman for their [HFA2k model](https://openmodeldb.info/models/4x-HFA2k) (included as "High Fidelity") - Foolhardy for their [Remacri model](https://openmodeldb.info/models/4x-Remacri). - [Kim2091](https://upscale.wiki/wiki/User:Kim2091) for their [Ultrasharp and Ultramix Balanced model](https://openmodeldb.info/models/4x-UltraSharp). - @NicKoehler for their amazing logo :) #
Copyright © 2023 - **Upscayl**\ By Nayam Amarshe and TGS963\ Made with 🖱 & ⌨

repositories.name: nvke
repositories.description: NVIDIA Kubernetes Engine (NVKE). A management plane for GPU Kubernetes on bare metal.
repositories.readme:
# NVIDIA Kubernetes Engine (NVKE)

[![License](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-Apache--2.0-blue.svg)](LICENSE)
[![Go](https://img.shields.io/badge/Go-1.27.3-00ADD8.svg)](go.work)

**Run a managed Kubernetes service on your own NVIDIA GPU infrastructure.**
NVIDIA Kubernetes® Engine (NVKE) provides the management plane that platform teams install to create and
operate Kubernetes clusters for their customers. Each workload cluster has its
own Kubernetes control plane, etcd and node pools. You operate the NVKE management
plane; your customers use their clusters through the Kubernetes API and `kubectl`.

> **Preview:** NVKE is available as a preview. APIs, configuration and behavior
> can change between releases, and we do not recommend NVKE for production
> workloads. See [Preview status and known limitations](docs/overview/preview-status.md).

[Get started](#getting-started) · [Documentation](docs/README.md) ·
[Contribute](CONTRIBUTING.md) · [Get help](SUPPORT.md)

## Getting started

| Your goal | Start here | What you get |
|---|---|---|
| **Evaluate without GPU hardware** | [Local quickstart](docs/get-started/quickstart-local.md) | A development management plane and a workload cluster on simulated machines. No NVIDIA account is required. |
| **Install on your infrastructure** | [Plan your installation](docs/operate/plan-installation.md) | The prerequisites and sequence for preparing nodes, bootstrapping a management cluster and installing its services. |
| **Build or contribute** | [Build from source](#build-from-source) | The NVKE binaries and the contributor development loop. |

The local quickstart runs on a **Linux host or VM, amd64 or arm64**, with at least
**6 CPUs, 12 GiB of free memory and 100 GiB of free disk**. It requires Docker,
virtual TPM support and the tools listed in the guide. Follow its setup through
workload-cluster creation and confirm the cluster's nodes report `Ready`.
On macOS, use the [local site guide](docs/get-started/local-site.md), which runs
the evaluation inside a Colima virtual machine.

For a real installation, you supply the machines, networking, node images and
registries, and configure access to **NVIDIA Infra Controller (NICo)**. NICo is
the sole compatible infrastructure provider at preview. The
[platform and version reference](docs/overview/supported-platforms.md) lists
validated combinations and pinned dependencies.

## What NVKE does

- **Creates independent workload clusters.** Request clusters through the NVKE
  API or `nvkectl`; NVKE provisions machines through NICo and forms Kubernetes
  clusters with their own control planes.
- **Manages workload cluster lifecycle.** Create, scale and delete node pools,
  upgrade Kubernetes and replace nodes. See the [node pool guide](docs/workload-clusters/node-pools.md)
  for the manual steps and preview limits on replacement and upgrades.
- **Establishes node identity.** Nodes attest through SPIFFE/SPIRE using their
  TPM before receiving join credentials. Encryption of etcd data is available
  per cluster.
- **Connects builds to deployment.** Its companion project,
  [NVIDIA Kubernetes Recipes (NVKR)](https://github.com/dsx-ai-factory/nvkr),
  builds node images and NVKE components from pinned inputs. NVKE deploys those
  artifacts; NVKR owns their build and release evidence.

The preview needs explicit operator configuration: API authentication is off
and the API uses plain HTTP after installation. Configure
[API authentication and protected access](docs/operate/api-authentication.md)
before admitting callers. The management cluster does not upgrade, scale or
replace itself, and there is no management-plane upgrade or backup/restore
procedure. FDE node images are for evaluation and provide no data-at-rest
confidentiality. Read the [known limitations](docs/overview/preview-status.md)
before choosing an evaluation or installation path.

## Overview

The diagram shows the NVKE product family, how it sits on NICo and your GPU machines, and which components talk to each other.

![NVKE product family. NVKR builds and signs artifacts and publishes them to a registry. The operator installs the management cluster's components, the NVKE management plane, CAPNICo and NVKE observability, from the charts and images in the registry. The management plane requests machines through CAPNICo, which calls NICo, and drives each workload cluster. NICo provisions NVIDIA GPU machines from the node OS image, and those machines become the workload cluster's Kubernetes nodes, each running nvke-agent, under the cluster's Kubernetes control plane. The accelerated runtime produced by AICR and NVKE observability are optional in the workload cluster. The customer uses kubectl against the control plane.](docs/assets/diagrams/product-family.svg)

NVKE is not a Kubernetes distribution and not a Cluster API flavour. It is a
**self-hosting factory for Kubernetes clusters**: a throwaway seed cluster
stands up a management cluster, and the management plane on
it then provisions and lifecycle-manages many isolated workload clusters
on demand.

An installation has two kinds of Kubernetes cluster:

- The **management cluster** runs the NVKE management plane and infrastructure
  controllers. `nvkectl` forms it using a temporary seed cluster; installing the
  management-plane services is a separate step.
- **Workload clusters** run customer applications. The management plane creates
  and operates them through NICo, Cluster API and the node agent.

Read [What is NVKE](docs/overview/what-is-nvke.md) for the operator workflow and
[Architecture](docs/architecture.md) for the implementation and data flows.

## Build from source

Use **Go 1.27.3**, the version pinned in [go.work](go.work), and **GNU Make 4 or later**. Public Go modules must be
reachable on the first build. [Flox](https://flox.dev/) is optional and supplies
the repository's development tools; on macOS, it also supplies GNU Make 4.
See [Development](docs/development.md) for toolchain setup.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/dsx-ai-factory/nvke.git
cd nvke
make build
```

This builds the workspace and writes nine binaries to `bin/`: `agent`,
`updater`, `controller`, `nvkectl`, `capd-reboot-controller`,
`nvke-os-image-check`, `management-engine`, `tenant-api` and `operator-api`. Building does not start a
management plane or create a cluster. The node agent runs on Linux.

The [workspace guide](docs/go-workspace.md) explains the modules and outputs.
For local services and test environments, see [Local development setup](docs/getting-started.md).
Before submitting a change, follow [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) and run
`make preflight`; it selects checks for the modules you changed.

## Documentation

| Task | Guide |
|---|---|
| Prepare nodes and bootstrap the management cluster | [Bootstrap the management cluster](docs/operate/bootstrap-management-cluster.md) |
| Install NVKE services | [Install the management plane from the deploy path](deploy/README.md) |
| Build node images and supply release artifacts | [Get NVKE artifacts from NVKR](docs/operate/build-node-images.md) |
| Create and manage customer clusters | [Create a workload cluster](docs/workload-clusters/create.md), [Manage node pools](docs/workload-clusters/node-pools.md) |
| Give a customer access | [Access a workload cluster](docs/workload-clusters/access.md) |
| Inspect cluster health and telemetry | [Observe NVKE and its clusters](docs/operate/observe.md) |

The [documentation index](docs/README.md) links the remaining guides and references.

## Contributing and support

Contributions, bug reports and documentation improvements are welcome.
Start with [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md); open an issue before substantial
work so maintainers can agree on the approach.

- **Questions:** [GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/dsx-ai-factory/nvke/discussions/categories/q-a).
- **Chat:** the `#nvke` channel in the DSX AI Factory Slack.
  [Get an invite](https://inviter.co/dsx-ai-factory).
- **Bugs and feature requests:** [GitHub Issues](https://github.com/dsx-ai-factory/nvke/issues).
- **Security vulnerabilities:** follow [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md) and report privately.
- **Community:** [Code of Conduct](CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md), [Governance](GOVERNANCE.md),
  [Maintainers](MAINTAINERS.md) and [Support](SUPPORT.md).
- **Releases:** [release process](RELEASE.md).
- **CI health:** the [CI dashboard](https://dsx-ai-factory.github.io/nvke/)
  shows the last thirty runs of every workflow and refreshes hourly.

## Trademarks

Kubernetes® is a registered trademark of The Linux Foundation in the United
States and other countries. NVIDIA and the NVIDIA logo are trademarks and/or
registered trademarks of NVIDIA Corporation in the U.S. and other countries.
Other company and product names may be trademarks of the respective companies
with which they are associated.

## License

repositories.description: Truly independent web browser
repositories.readme:
# Ladybird

[Ladybird](https://ladybird.org) is a truly independent web browser, using a novel engine based on web standards.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Ladybird is in a pre-alpha state, and only suitable for use by developers
>

## Features

We aim to build a complete, usable browser for the modern web.

Ladybird uses a [multi-process architecture](Documentation/ProcessArchitecture.md) with a main UI process,
WebContent renderer processes, and helper processes for tasks such as networking, image decoding, compositing and media.

Documents from different sites run in separate renderer processes, each sandboxed from the rest of the system.
Image decoding and network connections are done out of process, separately for each site, to be more robust against
malicious content.

At the moment, many core library support components are inherited from SerenityOS:

- LibWeb: Web rendering engine
- LibJS: JavaScript engine
- LibWasm: WebAssembly implementation
- LibCrypto/LibTLS: Cryptography primitives and Transport Layer Security
- LibHTTP: HTTP/1.1 client
- LibGfx: 2D Graphics Library, Image Decoding and Rendering
- LibUnicode: Unicode and locale support
- LibMedia: Audio and video playback
- LibCore: Event loop, OS abstraction layer
- LibIPC: Inter-process communication

## How do I build and run this?

See [build instructions](Documentation/BuildInstructionsLadybird.md) for information on how to build Ladybird.

Ladybird runs on Linux, macOS, Windows (with WSL2), and many other \*Nixes.

## How do I read the documentation?

Code-related documentation can be found in the [documentation](Documentation/) folder.

## Get in touch and participate!

Join [our Discord server](https://discord.gg/nvfjVJ4Svh) to participate in issue and development discussions.

Please read [Getting involved with Ladybird](Documentation/GettingStartedContributing.md) if you're new to Ladybird and want to help.

Before opening an issue, please see the [issue policy](CONTRIBUTING.md#issue-policy) and the [detailed issue-reporting guidelines](ISSUES.md).

The project participation guidelines can be found in [`CONTRIBUTING.md`](CONTRIBUTING.md).

## License

Ladybird is licensed under a 2-clause BSD license.
